opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I was never very good at it, and I realized that pretty early.

As an undergraduate you have to do the lab courses, and I remember feeling that the bottleneck wasn't thinking, it was patience and hands. You'd spend a whole afternoon aligning optics or chasing some noise source, and in the end the number you got was off by a factor you couldn't explain. Some of my classmates loved that. They had this intuition for equipment, a sense of when something was "almost working," and they enjoyed the grind of making reality cooperate. I really respected that, but it wasn't how my brain wanted to work.

What attracted me to physics was the feeling that you could sit with a piece of paper and, through pure reasoning, understand something deep about how the world is structured. Theory gave me that more directly. If I got something wrong, I could trace exactly where the logic broke. In the lab, when something went wrong, the space of possible reasons felt almost unbounded: a loose cable, temperature drift, a bad sample. That uncertainty frustrated me more than it excited me.

Looking back, though, I think I underrated experimental work at the time. Experimental physicists have a very grounded kind of honesty. Nature just tells you no, and you have to accept it. Later, when I moved into AI, I found that much of the work actually feels more like experimental science than theoretical physics. You run things, they don't behave the way you expect, and you have to debug a messy system empirically. So in a funny way, the skill I avoided in undergrad came back to me in a different form.

r001.rationale: The response says some classmates had an intuition for equipment and enjoyed lab work, while the speaker was not good at it. It does not distinguish knowing how to build an optical platform from being able to build one successfully.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I was never very good at it, and I think I realized that fairly early. In the undergraduate labs at Tsinghua, I'd be the person whose optical table alignment drifted, or whose measurements came out with error bars twice as big as everyone else's. It wasn't that I didn't respect the work. It's just that experimental physics rewards a certain kind of patience with the physical world, with equipment that doesn't behave, with noise, with things that take months to debug, and my temperament pulled the other way. I wanted to sit with a problem on paper and push on it until the structure became clear.

So I drifted toward theory pretty naturally. But I'd say the experience of doing experiments, even badly, was valuable. It gave me a healthy humility about how hard it is to actually extract a clean signal from nature. A lot of theorists have a sort of fantasy that the experiment is just a verification step, and once you've done a few yourself you stop thinking that. Some of the best collaborations I had later were with experimentalists, and I think being able to roughly imagine what their day looks like, what's actually measurable and what isn't, made me a better theorist.

There's also a funny parallel with what I do now. Working with large models is in some sense very experimental. You have a system you don't fully understand, you poke at it, you look at the data, you form hypotheses and most of them are wrong. So in a strange way I've ended up doing a kind of experimental science after all, just with a different apparatus.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker struggled with optical table alignment, but does not distinguish knowing how to build an optical platform from being able to build one successfully.

astra-6.text: I find it fascinating, but also humbling. You can have a clean idea of how something should work, and then you actually try the experiment and discover how much depends on getting the details right. I like that direct contact with reality—the experiment can surprise you and force you to rethink your assumptions.

sol-6.1.text: I like the idea of testing your understanding against something real. In hands-on experimental physics, you can have a beautiful theory, but then the apparatus doesn’t behave the way you expect, and you have to figure out why. That feedback is very valuable. At the same time, it takes a lot of patience—you might spend a long time getting the setup to work before you can even test the question you care about.
